items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
Selected trials that materially change clinical decisions in Set 16. The links open original trial reports, not secondary summaries. These trials do not establish a single treatment rule for every pain syndrome, and perioperative methadone/buprenorphine/naltrexone recommendations rely substantially on pharmacology, observational evidence and expert consensus rather than a definitive head-to-head RCT.

| **Trial — original paper** | **Primary finding** | **Final Exam interpretation / limitation** |
|---|---|---|
| [SPACE (Krebs et al., JAMA 2018)](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2673971) | 240 adults with chronic back or hip/knee osteoarthritis pain: an opioid strategy was not superior to nonopioid medication for pain-related function over 12 months. | Supports function-centred, nonopioid-first chronic non-cancer pain care. Excluded already opioid-dependent patients; do not generalise to acute major surgery, cancer or palliative care. |
| [I-WOTCH (Sandhu et al., JAMA 2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10208139/) | 608 adults taking long-term strong opioids: structured group education plus individual support increased opioid cessation at 12 months (29% vs 7%); pain interference did not differ significantly. | Supports voluntary, supported tapering with functional monitoring—not abrupt withdrawal. Discontinuation was self-reported, and applicability to unwilling or very high-dose patients is limited. |
| [RESTORE (Kent et al., Lancet 2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37146623/) | 492 people with chronic disabling low-back pain: individualised cognitive functional therapy, with or without sensor feedback, improved activity limitation versus usual care at 13 weeks; benefits persisted to 52 weeks. | Supports psychologically informed movement rehabilitation. Specific trained therapy and low-back population; 3-year follow-up had attrition and does not prove efficacy for every persistent-pain syndrome. |
| [STarT Back (Hill et al., Lancet 2011)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21963002/) | 851 primary-care patients with low-back pain: risk-stratified care matched to a screening tool improved disability modestly at 4 and 12 months compared with best current care. | Demonstrates value of prognostic/psychosocial assessment and matched treatment intensity; specific primary-care pathway, not a universal hospital pain score or drug algorithm. |
| [PRECISE (Mathieson et al., NEJM 2017)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28328324/) | In acute or chronic sciatica, pregabalin did not significantly reduce leg-pain intensity versus placebo at 8 weeks and caused more adverse events. | Avoid equating radicular sciatica with every peripheral neuropathic pain syndrome. Does not disprove all gabapentinoid benefit for other indicated neuropathic conditions. |
| [OPAL (Jones et al., Lancet 2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37392748/) | 347 adults with acute nonspecific low-back or neck pain: adding short-course oxycodone–naloxone to guideline care did not improve pain at 6 weeks versus placebo. | Avoid routine opioids for uncomplicated nonspecific spinal pain. Does not apply directly to fracture, ischaemia, major operative injury or severe cancer pain. |

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## Evidence audit and scope

The **Prioritised Learning Sets (5)** workbook contains **15 rows**, of which **14 are complete outcomes** and **one is a specifically assigned component** of the wider perioperative-medicine parent. Its overview says “21 explicit components consolidated into 15 parent rows”. The mapping below is based on the actual 15 rows in the Set 16 sheet and the corresponding Appendix Five outcomes in **ANZCA Anaesthesia Training Program Curriculum v1.14 (December 2025)**. A reference to a chapter means a substantive teaching section, not a tick-box list.

**Depth certification for this document:** every allocated Set 16 code has (a) an explanation of its mechanism/clinical context, (b) the relevant recognition/assessment or comparative decision, and (c) an explicit management strategy or safety implication at the level implied by **define / outline / describe / discuss / formulate**. The P1 material is deliberately deeper than the P5 definitions. This crosswalk establishes written teaching coverage, not mastery, examination success or a claim that every general anaesthetic/obstetric/regional/ICU outcome is repeated here. The separately maintained SAQ/Retrieve/Speak banks remain independent and were not re-audited.

**Consolidation note.** The following are intentionally not taught as new complete Set 16 outcomes: comprehensive acute pain/PCA/epidural techniques (Set 15), entire cardiovascular/renal/endocrine perioperative disease management (their assigned sets), advanced obstetric analgesia, general regional anatomy and all types of chronic headache or palliative cancer care. Set 16 teaches the opioid-tolerant and persistent-pain interfaces required here, with explicit ownership boundaries and high-priority cross-set integration.

## Linked references and source register

**How references were used:** Official ANZCA/FPM position statements, the supplied curriculum and current major guidelines were consulted for their relevant recommendations. Selected BJA Education papers and primary published reviews were used for educational mechanisms and evidence context. References below are **linked source records and targeted evidence checks, not a representation that every accessible full-text PDF or every chapter of a textbook was re-read**. Exam-report references arise from the supplied official files and are historical examiner emphases; they are not automatically 2026 prescribing instructions.

- **[R1] ANZCA/FPM, PS45 — Position statement on patients’ rights to pain management and associated responsibilities (2025).** Primary position statement: [ANZCA professional documents](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents). Use: person-centred assessment, validation, equity, evidence–harm balance and transitions; position rather than prescriptive drug choice.
- **[R2] FPM ANZCA, PS01(PM) — Statement regarding opioid analgesics in chronic non-cancer pain (2025).** [Official document](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/7d7d2619-6736-4d8e-876e-6f9b2b45c435/PS01%28PM%29-Statement-regarding-the-use-of-opioid-analgesics-in-patients-with-chronic-non-cancer-pain). Use: exceptional opioid role, self-management, functional evidence of benefit, harm surveillance and take-home naloxone thresholds.
- **[R3] NICE NG193 — Chronic pain (primary and secondary): assessment and chronic primary pain management.** [Recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng193/chapter/recommendations). Use: chronic primary versus secondary, person-centred assessment, supervised exercise, ACT/CBT and condition-specific pharmacology.
- **[R4] FPM ANZCA, PS17(PM) — Multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary care in specialist pain services (pilot launched 22 October 2026).** [Launch and scope](https://prod-anzca-094930.xperience-sites.com/news-and-safety-alerts/ps17%28pm%29-multidisciplinary-and-interdisciplinary-care-in-specialist-pain-services-and-pain-units). Use: coordinated specialist team practice; status is **pilot**, not final binding regulation.
- [R5] Gauntlett-Gilbert J, Brook P. “Living well with chronic pain: the role of pain-management programmes.” BJA Education 2018;18:3–7 (online 2017). [Full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807918/). Use: self-management, rehabilitation, team integration and risks of repeated rescue medicalisation.
- [R6] Gallagher H, Galvin D. “Opioids for chronic non-cancer pain.” BJA Education 2018;18:337–341. [Full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808073/). Use: opioid benefits/harms and chronic-prescribing limitations; modern policy from PS01(PM).
- **[R7] NICE NG59 — Low back pain and sciatica in over-16s, recommendations, updated 29 July 2026.** [Recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng59/chapter/Recommendations) and [update statement](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng59/chapter/Update-information). Use: triage, activity, drug treatment, radicular versus non-specific pain and **psychology recommendation withdrawal nuance**.
- **[R8] UK Faculty of Pain Medicine — Statement on July 2026 NICE NG59 update.** [Faculty statement](https://www.fpm.ac.uk/fpm-position-statement-july-2026-update-nice-ng59). Use: deletion ≠ a recommendation against psychological/MDT care; consider NG193 and wider chronic-pain evidence.
- **[R9] NICE CG173 — Neuropathic pain in adults: pharmacological management.** [Recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg173/chapter/Recommendations). Use: neuropathic medicine selection/review, early referral and trigeminal-neuralgia exception; **exclude sciatica** from uncritical application.
- **[R10] Murnion B et al. “Opioid use disorder in anaesthesia and intensive care: prevention, diagnosis and management.” Anaesthesia and Intensive Care (2022).** [Publisher review](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0310057X211066929). Use: diagnosis, perioperative OUD, opioid agonist treatment and clinician harm reduction.
- **[R11] Multisociety expert panel — Buprenorphine management in the perioperative period (2021).** [ASRA summary](https://asra.com/news-publications/asra-updates/blog-landing/guidelines/2021/08/12/buprenorphine-management-in-the-perioperative-period) and [primary consensus](https://rapm.bmj.com/content/early/2021/08/11/rapm-2021-103007). Use: do not routinely stop buprenorphine, use multimodal analgesia, plan discharge with MOUD prescriber.
- **[R12] Harrison TK et al. “Perioperative considerations for medications for opioid use disorder: buprenorphine, methadone or naltrexone.” Anesthesiology Clinics 2025.** [PubMed record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41233100/). Use: drug-specific planning; source review access may be abstract/index rather than entire subscription text.
- **[R13] FPM ANZCA, historical and current chronic opioid pharmacology background.** See the BJA Education opioid review [R6] and PS01(PM) [R2]; cited separately in chapter narrative to contrast **education** and **current prescribing statement**. This is not claimed to be an additional independent publication.
- [R14] Rosenberger DC, Pogatzki-Zahn EM. “Chronic post-surgical pain—update on incidence, risk factors and preventive treatment options.” BJA Education 2022;22:190–196. [Full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9039436/). Use: CPSP definition, biopsychosocial risk, perioperative predictors and evidence limitations.
- **[R15] FPM ANZCA, PS11(PM) — Procedures in Pain Medicine Clinical Care Standard (2020).** [ANZCA standards index](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/standards-for-pain-medicine). Use: procedure selection, governance, consent and rescue expectations for neurolysis/interventional pain.
- [R16] Royds J, McCrory C. “Neuroimmunity and chronic pain.” BJA Education 2018;18:377–383. [Full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808040/). Use: glial/neuroimmune pathways; mechanism—not a stand-alone clinical diagnostic test.
- [R17] Cox JJ, Srivastava D. “The genetics of pain.” BJA Education 2024;24:417–425. [Full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11602659/). Use: biological heterogeneity and genetic influences, supplementary rather than a daily prescribing algorithm.
- [R18] Whately Y, Stead M. “Perioperative management of patients on naltrexone.” Australasian Anaesthesia (ANZCA Blue Book) 2023:103–112. [ANZCA repository](https://airr.anzca.edu.au/anzcacrisjspui/handle/11055/1180). Use: antagonist blockade, monitoring, nonopioid strategies and safe restart; distinguish local practice from generalisable evidence.
- **[R19] ANZCA official Final Examination Chair’s reports (provided in this project): 2025.2 (Q14 naltrexone), 2020.1 (Q5 naltrexone), 2021.1 (Q8 long-term opioids).** Source documents: 2025.2 Final Examination Report.pdf, FEX 2020.1.pdf, 2021.1 Final Exam Report.pdf. Use: priorities and common examiner errors, not an exhaustive historical SAQ reconciliation.
- **[R20] European Pain Federation — Budapest CRPS criteria** [clinical checklist](https://crps.europeanpainfederation.eu/budapest-criteria/); additional [2025 Pain Practice CRPS review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11680468/). Use: formal CRPS diagnostic categories, alternative causes and early rehabilitation.
- **[R21] “Chronic postsurgical pain: risk assessment and mitigation” (2026 review).** [PubMed record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42479827/). Use: recent risk/mitigation context; bibliographic/abstract scope, not represented as a full-text review.
- **[R22] ANZCA PS41(G) — Position statement on acute pain management (2023).** [Official document](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/136f5a83-d1d0-4f34-be72-87b62b721d14/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/PS41%28G%29-Position-statement-on-acute-pain-management-2023.PDF). Use: acute pain assessment, stewardship, special populations, monitoring and safe care transitions.
- **[R23] Burns SL et al. “Perioperative Anesthetic Management of Opioid Tolerant Patients and Patients with Active and Medically Treated Opioid Use Disorder.” Current Opinion in Anaesthesiology (2022).** [Full-text review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9308736/). Used for practical perioperative reconciliation and monitoring, maintenance versus rescue analgesia and antagonist timing; apply current local protocols.
- **[R24] “Narrative review: Managing buprenorphine and opioid use disorder in the perioperative setting” (2024).** [Full-text review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11683522/). Used for continuation, discharge, overdose prevention and coordination, not as a mandatory fixed-dose protocol.
- [R25] Society of Hospital Medicine. “Management of Opioid Use Disorder and Associated Conditions among Hospitalized Adults” (2022). [Consensus statement](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9474708/). Used for maintaining agonist therapy and coordinating medication and discharge safely; recommendations are adapted to the ANZCA/local setting.
- [R26] American Society of Addiction Medicine. “Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management” (2020). [Official guideline](https://www.asam.org/quality-care/clinical-guidelines/alcohol-withdrawal-management-guideline). Used for withdrawal risk, scale limitations, benzodiazepine-first-line treatment, thiamine and monitoring; local Australasian protocols take precedence for dosing and resources.
- **[R27] ANZCA/FPM and perioperative toxicology principles.** Substance-specific mechanisms and emergency management are educational synthesis from established perioperative pharmacology and clinical toxicology; not represented as a separately fully reviewed ANZCA guideline. Follow local toxicology/anaesthetic advice for acute stimulant toxicity and unfamiliar exposure.
- **[R28] Perioperative psychotropic pharmacology teaching.** Anxiety/depression, antipsychotic, lithium and antidepressant decisions are educational synthesis, reflecting medication-specific risks; no universal preoperative interruption rule is asserted. Check the actual product, current institutional guidance and psychiatry input where required.

**Curriculum sources (provided):** training program curriculum.pdf (version 1.14, Appendix Five, Pain Medicine and relevant perioperative-medicine outcomes); Prioritised LEarning Sets(5).xlsx, worksheet 16 Persistent Pain, detailed rows 4–18. The source workbook has not been altered; its statuses remain user-controlled.

- [R29] [SPACE (Krebs et al., JAMA 2018)](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2673971). Original randomised trial. See the linked landmark-trials comparison above for population, primary finding, limits and exam relevance.
- [R30] [I-WOTCH (Sandhu et al., JAMA 2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10208139/). Original randomised trial. See the linked landmark-trials comparison above for population, primary finding, limits and exam relevance.
- [R31] [RESTORE (Kent et al., Lancet 2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37146623/). Original randomised trial. See the linked landmark-trials comparison above for population, primary finding, limits and exam relevance.
- [R32] [STarT Back (Hill et al., Lancet 2011)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21963002/). Original randomised trial. See the linked landmark-trials comparison above for population, primary finding, limits and exam relevance.
- [R33] [PRECISE (Mathieson et al., NEJM 2017)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28328324/). Original randomised trial. See the linked landmark-trials comparison above for population, primary finding, limits and exam relevance.
- [R34] [OPAL (Jones et al., Lancet 2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37392748/). Original randomised trial. See the linked landmark-trials comparison above for population, primary finding, limits and exam relevance.
